name: The three branches of jyotiṣa (skandha-traya)

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa rests on three branches: gaṇita or siddhānta (computation of the planets' motions), horā (nativities) and saṃhitā (omens and mundane matters); Parāśara calls the horā the best of the three; Varāhamihira composed works in all three.
Kerala authors speak of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga): nativity (jātaka), sphere (gola), omens (nimitta), interrogation (praśna), electional timing (muhūrta) and computation (gaṇita).

notes: The six-limb list is from memory (Praśna Mārga ch. 1) and is low confidence.

name: Jyotiṣa as the eye of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Vedas exist for the sacrifices, which depend on times; so the science of time is the eye (cakṣus, nayana) of the Veda and stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas like a peacock's crest; Parāśara calls his horā the 'eye of the Veda heard from Brahmā's mouth', says none can know past and future without it, and warns that one who condemns it goes to hell.

relations.note: jyotiṣa is one of the six limbs

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: the science is not man-made — the Sun taught it to Maya through a portion of himself, the same śāstra told to the seers in every age with only the time-difference changing (SS 1.2–9); Āryabhaṭa raised it from the ocean of knowledge by Brahmā's grace (Āryabhaṭīya 4.49); Parāśara tells it as heard from Brahmā (BPHS 1.6); later lists name eighteen promulgators.

name: The eighteen promulgators of jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: Later saṃhitās (e.g. those of Nārada and Kaśyapa) list eighteen originators of jyotiṣa: Sūrya, Pitāmaha, Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Parāśara, Kaśyapa, Nārada, Garga, Marīci, Manu, Aṅgiras, Lomaśa, Pauliśa, Cyavana, Yavana, Bhṛgu and Śaunaka.

notes: List recalled from memory; its source verse and exact membership vary by text. Check before use.

name: Teacher, pupil and the handing down of jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa passes from teacher to pupil, often father to son (Varāhamihira from Ādityadāsa; Gaṇeśa from Keśava; Rāma and Nīlakaṇṭha from Ananta), and is given only to the calm, devoted, truthful believer — never to another's pupil, an unbeliever or a cheat (BPHS 1.7–8). The secret chapter is withheld from none who is very devoted (SS 12.11). Authors bow to the former promulgators and do not discard their works (BJ 28.10; BS 105.2); counterfeiting the text destroys merit and life (Āryabhaṭīya 4.50); even foreign Yavanas who master it are honoured like seers (BS 2.14).

The astrologer (sāṃvatsara, daivajña) must be of good family, pleasing, learned in all three branches, pure, skilled and eloquent (BS 2); only a seer crosses the ocean of Kālapuruṣa (BS 2.4); the king must honour him, and even forest-dwelling renunciants consult him (BS 2.6–8); one who predicts by trickery, feigned possession or eavesdropping is no knower of fate (BS 2.15); the Kerala manual requires daily worship, recitation and truthfulness of him (Praśna Mārga 1).

name: The ultimate as named in jyotiṣa texts

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa texts name the ultimate in their invocations and cosmogonies rather than teach it: Brahman, unthinkable and unmanifest, without and with qualities (SS 1.1); Vāsudeva the supreme Brahman, from whom Saṅkarṣaṇa, the golden egg and Aniruddha-as-Sun arise (SS 12.12–21); Ka, one and many, the supreme Brahman (Āryabhaṭīya 1.1); Viṣṇu, one and unmanifest, with his three powers (BPHS 1.9–20); the Sun as self of all and door of liberation (Yogayātrā 1.1; BJ 1.1); for the Bṛhat Saṃhitā the ultimate cause is disputed among Kapila, Kaṇāda and those who say time, nature or karma (BS 1.7).

name: The Sun as the self of time and of beings

definitions.definition: The Sun is the self (ātman) of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 2.1), the self of all embodied beings, maker of time and the opened door of liberation (Yogayātrā 1.1), the path of those not reborn and the self of the self-knowers (BJ 1.1), the Hiraṇyagarbha, the 'self of time and maker of time' whose chariot-wheel is the year (SS 12.15–19).

name: Self and mind in the chart

definitions.definition: In horā the Sun signifies the self (ātman) and the Moon the mind (manas) of Kālapuruṣa, Mercury speech, Jupiter knowledge, Venus desire and Saturn sorrow (BJ 2.1); firmness comes from the Sun and bodily-mental nature from the Moon (BS 68.3); the planet with the highest degrees is the significator of the self (ātmakāraka) (Jaimini 1.1.11; BPHS 32.3); all beings have a jīva-portion and a supreme-Self portion (BPHS 1.21–24).

name: The jīva-portion and the supreme-Self portion

definitions.definition: Every being contains two portions, of the individual soul and of the supreme Self; in the planets, the gods' powers and the full avatāras (Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Narasiṃha, Varāha) the supreme-Self portion predominates, in men the jīva-portion; the avatāras come forth from the planets and return into them, and beings finally merge into the unmanifest (BPHS 1.21–24; 2.1–10).

name: The body and constitution in the chart

definitions.definition: The twelve signs are the limbs of Kālapuruṣa from head to feet (BJ 1.4); each planet has a constitution — the Sun pitta, the Moon vāta and kapha, Mercury all three — a colour, a caste and an element (BJ 2.4–9); the five great men are known by bodily marks and measures (BS 68); the Vāstu-man is a body laid over every site (BS 52.2–3).

The Moon, Sun and Jupiter are of sattva, Mercury and Venus of rajas, Mars and Saturn of tamas (BJ 2.7); a person's predominant guṇa shows in conduct — compassion and devotion (sattva), arts, sacrifice and passion (rajas), deceit, sloth and anger (tamas) — with seven mixed kinds (BS 68.8–9); BPHS 77 gives the fruits of the guṇas.

relations.note: jyotiṣa assigns the three guṇas of the common (Sāṃkhya) teaching to the planets

definitions.definition: In jyotiṣa the three qualities are distributed among the planets — Moon, Sun and Jupiter sattva; Mercury and Venus rajas; Mars and Saturn tamas — and read in a person's conduct (BJ 2.7; BS 68.8–9).

name: The planets and the five elements

definitions.definition: From Brahmā's mind came the moon and from his eyes the sun; then Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn were born from fire, earth, ether, water and air (SS 12.22–24), and Varāhamihira makes them the lords of these elements (BJ 2.6).

The seven visible planets — Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn — with the two nodes Rāhu and Ketu make the nine grahas; they are forms of Janārdana giving the fruits of karma, and from them the avatāras are born (BPHS 2.3–7); their synonyms include Greek-derived names (BJ 2.2–3); they are worshipped together in the planetary sacrifice (YājñSm 1.295–308; BPHS 84).

name: What the planets signify (kārakatva)

definitions.definition: Each planet signifies parts of the person and world: the Sun the self and father and kingship, the Moon mind and mother, Mars strength and siblings, Mercury speech and learning, Jupiter knowledge, children and teachers, Venus desire and spouse, Saturn sorrow, servants and longevity (BJ 2.1 and later texts).

notes: Beyond BJ 2.1 the list follows common later texts (BPHS 32; Phaladīpikā 2) from memory.

definitions.definition: A planet's strength depends on its placement: exaltation at a fixed degree and fall in the seventh sign from it (BJ 1.13), root-trine sign, own sign, friendly and enemy signs, and vargottama.

name: Natural and temporary friendship of planets

definitions.definition: Planets are by nature friends, neutrals or enemies of one another, and become temporary friends when placed in the 2nd–4th and 10th–12th from each other; the combination gives five grades of relationship used in judging strength and in marriage matching (grahamaitra).

notes: From standard horā teaching (BJ 2.15–17; BPHS 3); verse references not checked.

definitions.definition: Every planet aspects the seventh house fully and the 3rd/10th, 5th/9th and 4th/8th with one, two and three quarters; Saturn, Jupiter and Mars have full aspect on these respectively (BJ 2.13).

relations.note: Parāśarī planetary aspect vs Jaimini sign-aspect; both are taught side by side in BPHS

definitions.definition: In the Jaimini system signs, not planets, aspect: each sign sees the sign facing it and those at its sides, so movable signs aspect the fixed signs except the adjacent, fixed signs the movable except the adjacent, and dual signs one another (Jaimini 1.1.2–3; BPHS 8).

The Lord divided himself twelvefold as the signs (SS 12.25); the signs are the limbs of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4), alternately odd/male/cruel and even/female/gentle, movable, fixed and dual in turn, each with a planetary lord, an alternative Greek-derived name (BJ 1.8) and a figure (BJ 1.5).

Time imagined as a person: the signs are his limbs from head to feet (BJ 1.4), the Sun his self, the Moon his mind and so on (BJ 2.1); his ocean cannot be crossed even in mind by one who is not a seer (BS 2.4). An affliction to a sign afflicts the corresponding limb of the native.

name: The twelve houses and their significations

definitions.definition: Counted from the ascendant, the houses signify: 1 body and self (tanu); 2 wealth, family and speech; 3 siblings and courage; 4 mother, home, happiness; 5 children, intellect and merit of past lives; 6 enemies, disease, debt; 7 spouse; 8 longevity and death; 9 fortune, dharma, teacher and father; 10 action and position; 11 gains; 12 loss, expense and liberation (BJ 1.15–16; BPHS 11–23).

notes: Significations beyond BJ's house-names follow standard later texts (BPHS 11–23) from memory.

name: Groupings of houses

definitions.definition: Angles (kendra: 1, 4, 7, 10), succedents (paṇaphara: 2, 5, 8, 11) and cadents (āpoklima: 3, 6, 9, 12); trines (1, 5, 9); increasing houses (upacaya: 3, 6, 10, 11); bad houses (duḥsthāna: 6, 8, 12); death-dealing houses (2 and 7) (BJ 1.15–18; BPHS 44). Later practitioners also group the houses by the four aims of life (dharma 1-5-9, artha 2-6-10, kāma 3-7-11, mokṣa 4-8-12).

notes: The four-aims grouping is modern-popular; classical source not located.

name: The twenty-seven (twenty-eight) lunar mansions and their deities

definitions.definition: The moon's path is divided into 27 asterisms of 13°20′ (28 with Abhijit in muhūrta), each with a presiding deity; the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa lists them from Kṛttikā (Agni) to Bharaṇī (Yama), later texts from Aśvinī (the Aśvins) to Revatī (Pūṣan); the Lord divided himself into them (SS 12.25).
The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna expounds the asterisms, their deities and the fortunes of those born under them, in the mouth of the outcaste king Triśaṅku.

name: Classes of asterisms for action

definitions.definition: For choosing times the asterisms are grouped by nature, each group paired with a weekday: fixed (dhruva), movable (cara), fierce (ugra), mixed (miśra), swift/light (kṣipra), soft (mṛdu) and sharp (tīkṣṇa); each suits particular undertakings (BS 97.6–9; MC 2.2–8).

members: cara: Svātī, Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj

definitions.definition: In sacrificial rites the sacrificer bears a name derived from his asterism (VJ r.28); later practice assigns a syllable to each asterism-quarter for choosing a child's name.

Each sign is divided into equal parts ruled by planets, each division forming a chart for a domain of life: six in Varāhamihira (BJ 1.9), sixteen 'spoken by Brahmā' in Parāśara — sign, horā, drekkāṇa, fourth, seventh, navāṃśa, tenth, twelfth, sixteenth, twentieth, twenty-fourth, twenty-seventh, thirtieth, fortieth, forty-fifth and sixtieth (BPHS 6.2–4).

Seven (or eight, with Rāhu) planets ranked by their degrees in their signs become the significators of self, minister, brother, mother, son, kin and wife; the highest is the ātmakāraka (Jaimini 1.1.11; BPHS 32.1–4).

Life unfolds through periods ruled by planets or signs: Varāhamihira's periods of planets placed in angles, succedents and cadents (BJ 8); Parāśara's many systems — asterism-based (Viṃśottarī, Aṣṭottarī, Ṣoḍaśottarī …), sign-based (Cara, Sthira, Nārāyaṇa …), Kālacakra, Yoginī and others — 'not all accepted by all' (BPHS 46.3–11).

The 120-year system counted from the birth-asterism: the lords, repeating thrice from Kṛttikā, are the Sun (6 years), Moon (10), Mars (7), Rāhu (18), Jupiter (16), Saturn (19), Mercury (17), Ketu (7) and Venus (20); since a full life is 120 years it is chief in the Kali age (BPHS 46.12–15).

name: The Aṣṭottarī period system

definitions.definition: A 108-year asterism-based system of eight planets (without Ketu): Sun 6, Moon 15, Mars 8, Mercury 17, Saturn 10, Jupiter 19, Rāhu 12, Venus 21 years; applied under particular conditions (BPHS 46–47).

notes: Years and order from memory.

name: The Yoginī period system

definitions.definition: A 36-year cycle of eight yoginīs — Maṅgalā (1 year), Piṅgalā (2), Dhānyā (3), Bhrāmarī (4), Bhadrikā (5), Ulkā (6), Siddhā (7) and Saṅkaṭā (8) — ruled by Moon, Sun, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Saturn, Venus and Rāhu, reckoned from the birth-asterism (named in BPHS 46.10).

notes: Names and planet-assignments from memory.

name: The Cara (sign) period system

definitions.definition: In the Jaimini system the periods belong to signs, counted forward or backward from the ascendant according to the sign's nature, each lasting as many years as its lord is distant from it (Jaimini 2; BPHS 50).

notes: Rules summarized from memory; chapter references not checked.

definitions.definition: A yoga is a configuration giving a definite fruit; the Yavanas counted 1,800 nābhasa yogas (BJ 12.1); the main families are royal (rāja), wealth (dhana), poverty (daridra), the five great men, lunar yogas, nābhasa yogas, renunciation (pravrajyā) and misfortune (ariṣṭa).

Combinations making the native a king or kingly: by exalted planets in Varāhamihira (the Yavanas say exalted malefics make a cruel king, Jīvaśarman denies they make a king at all: BJ 11.1); by the relation of the lords of angles and trines, the yogakāraka, and the cancelled fall (nīcabhaṅga) in Parāśara (BPHS 34, 39–40).

name: Combinations for wealth and poverty

definitions.definition: Relations of the lords of the 2nd, 11th, 5th and 9th houses give wealth; afflictions of those houses and lords give poverty (BPHS 41–42).

notes: Chapter-level; rules summarized from memory.

definitions.definition: When Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus or Saturn is strong in its own sign or exaltation in an angle, one of the five great men is born — Rucaka, Bhadra, Haṃsa, Mālavya, Śaśa — each with his bodily marks and measures (BS 68; BPHS 75).

name: Lunar combinations

definitions.definition: Planets (other than the Sun) in the 2nd from the Moon give sunaphā, in the 12th anaphā, in both durudharā; none on either side gives the ill kemadruma (BJ 13); Jupiter in an angle from the Moon gives gajakesarī (later texts); benefics in the 6th, 7th and 8th from the Moon give adhi yoga.

notes: BJ 13 content from memory; not spot-checked. Scholarly account: sunaphā, anaphā, durudharā and kemadruma are Greek-derived terms.

name: The nābhasa ('sky') yogas

definitions.definition: Configurations formed by the pattern of all the planets: the Yavanas counted 1,800; Varāhamihira gives the three āśraya yogas (rajju, musala, nala), the two dala yogas (mālā, sarpa — taught by Parāśara), and the ākṛti and saṅkhyā yogas — thirty-two in all; they give their fruits in all periods (BJ 12).

notes: The 3+2+20+7 = 32 count is from memory.

definitions.definition: Four or more strong planets in one sign make a renunciant; the strongest decides the order — for Varāhamihira Śākya, Ājīvika, bhikṣu, vṛddha, caraka, nirgrantha or forest-dweller (BJ 15.1), for Parāśara tapasvin, kāpālika, red-robed, ekadaṇḍin, yati, cakradhara or nirgrantha (BPHS 79.2–3); a planet set in the sun gives devotion without initiation; Saturn's aspect gives initiation; certain royal yogas make a founder of a holy place (BJ 15.2–4).

relations.note: renunciation-yogas and the signs of liberation are distinct: the first shows entering an order, the second the final state

definitions.definition: The span of life is computed from the planets — by the methods of Maya, the Yavanas, Maṇittha and Parāśara (exaltation-years halved in fall), of Jīvaśarman, and of Satya (by navāṃśas traversed), whom Varāhamihira prefers (BJ 7); the lords of the 2nd and 7th are the killers (māraka) whose periods bring death when life is spent (BPHS 44).

name: Manner of death and the next world in the chart

definitions.definition: The eighth house and the 22nd decan show the manner of death (BJ 25.1–11); the lord of the decan occupied by the stronger luminary shows the world one came from — gods (Jupiter), fathers (Moon, Venus), animals (Sun, Mars) or hell-beings (Saturn, Mercury) (BJ 25.14) — and the lords of the 6th/8th decans or planets in the 7th the world one goes to (BJ 25.15).

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic/Gītā paths after death are by knowledge and time of death; horā reads the destination from the chart

definitions.definition: In jyotiṣa, early death is foretold by ariṣṭa yogas at birth (BJ 6; BPHS 9) and a king's death by portents such as images weeping or sweating (BS 45.8); longevity is computed and the killing planets identified (BJ 7; BPHS 44).

name: Signs of liberation in the chart

definitions.definition: Horā names configurations indicating liberation: Jupiter exalted in the 6th, an angle or the 8th, or the 12th rising in a benefic navāṃśa with the other planets weak (BJ 25.15); the kārakāṃśa exalted gives constancy in dharma and kaivalya, and Ketu in the twelfth from it gives kaivalya (Jaimini 1.2.13, 1.2.69).

name: The chart reveals the ripening of past karma

definitions.definition: The horā reveals the ripening of the karma, good and bad, earned in a former birth (BJ 1.3); the science shows it as a lamp shows objects in the dark (LJ 1.3); Janārdana in the form of the planets gives beings the fruits of their karma (BPHS 2.3); sins of former births appear as childlessness and other afflictions (BPHS 83).

relations.note: the karma 'earned in a former birth' now ripening, which the chart shows, corresponds to what Vedānta calls prārabdha; the jyotiṣa texts do not use the threefold classification themselves

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa does not itself classify karma threefold, but teaches that the chart reveals the ripening of karma earned in former births (BJ 1.3; LJ 1.3) — the portion later practitioners identify with prārabdha.

name: The planets as avatāras of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: Janārdana takes the form of the planets to give beings the fruits of karma; to destroy the daityas, strengthen the gods and establish dharma, the avatāras were born from the planets: Rāma from the Sun, Kṛṣṇa from the Moon, Narasiṃha from Mars, the Buddha from Mercury, Vāmana from Jupiter, Paraśurāma from Venus, the Tortoise from Saturn, the Boar from Rāhu and the Fish from Ketu (BPHS 2.3–7).

Fate (daiva) is karma made in another birth; success comes from fate and human effort together, like a harvest from rain and ploughing; a single defect ruins all (Yogayātrā 1.3–4). Favourable planets alone do not bring success, or the astrologer would be king; rites alone do not, or the priest would be king (1.5–6). Yet an act begun under ill-placed planets destroys its doer, and a well-timed one succeeds with slight effort (BS 103.59–60). The smṛti says fate is human effort of a former body and a chariot does not move on one wheel (YājñSm 1.349–351).

relations.note: both the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and Varāhamihira call fate one's own former action; they differ in weight — the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha makes present effort all-powerful, Varāhamihira requires both

definitions.definition: In jyotiṣa, fate is karma made in another birth, and success needs fate and human effort together like farming; neither favourable planets nor rites alone suffice (Yogayātrā 1.3–6); the smṛti likewise calls fate the effort of a former body (YājñSm 1.349–351).

Because the happiness and sorrow of creatures depend on the planets, their sacrifice is to be performed for peace, prosperity, rain, long life and nourishment (BPHS 84.1–3; YājñSm 1.295–308): images, Vedic mantras, fuel-sticks, food, gifts, recitation and worship for each planet; pacification rites for births at eclipses, junctions, Mūla and Viṣṭi (BPHS 86–96); gifts, cow-milking at a Rudra shrine and the ten-million oblation for portents (BS 45.4–7); gems examined for their fortune (BS 79.1); expiations for curses of past lives (BPHS 83; Praśna Mārga). Varāhamihira warns that rites alone do not bring success (Yogayātrā 1.6).

name: Correspondences of the nine planets

definitions.definition: Each planet has its own image-material, colour, mount and weapons (BPHS 84.4–13), its fuel-stick and gift (YājñSm 1.295–306), and in later texts its gem: ruby (Sun), pearl (Moon), coral (Mars), emerald (Mercury), yellow sapphire (Jupiter), diamond (Venus), blue sapphire (Saturn), hessonite (Rāhu) and cat's-eye (Ketu).

notes: The planet–gem table is from later texts (commonly Phaladīpikā 2); the Bṛhat Saṃhitā's gem chapters do not assign gems to planets.

definitions.definition: Time is twofold: the time that ends the worlds, and reckonable time, gross (embodied, from the breath) and subtle (unembodied, from the truṭi) (SS 1.10–11); time is without beginning or end and is inferred from the planets and stars (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11).

In jyotiṣa time is twofold — the destroyer of worlds and measurable time, gross and subtle (SS 1.10–11) — beginningless and endless, inferred from the planets (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11); the Sun is its self and maker (SS 12.18; Yogayātrā 1.1).

Units from the prāṇa (the time of a breath) and vināḍī to the nāḍī, the sidereal and civil day, lunar and solar months, the year which is a day of the gods (SS 1.11–14), up to the yuga and kalpa; nine kinds of measure are distinguished — of Brahmā, the gods, the fathers, Prajāpati, Jupiter, the sun, the civil day, the moon and the stars (SS 14).

name: The yugas and kalpa in the siddhāntas

definitions.definition: The caturyuga of 4,320,000 solar years is divided 4:3:2:1 by the feet of dharma; 71 caturyugas and a junction make a manvantara; 14 manvantaras and junctions make a kalpa of 1,000 caturyugas, a day of Brahmā, whose life is 100 years, half now passed (SS 1.15–21). Āryabhaṭa instead makes the four quarters equal and the kalpa 14 × 72 yugas (Āryabhaṭīya 1.5), which Brahmagupta rejects as contrary to smṛti (BSS 1.9).

relations.note: the siddhāntic figures in solar years restate the smṛti's divine-year scheme (MDh 1.68–80) with the same proportions (Āryabhaṭa excepted)

name: The ages, the Manu-periods and the day of Brahmā

definitions.definition: The siddhāntas compute the caturyuga as 4,320,000 solar years divided 4:3:2:1, 71 caturyugas to a manvantara and 1,000 to a kalpa (SS 1.15–21; BSS 1.7–9); Āryabhaṭa alone makes the four quarters equal (Āryabhaṭīya 1.5, 3.9).

name: The epoch of the Kali age

definitions.definition: The siddhāntas count days from the beginning of the Kali age (by their reckoning 3102 BCE); Āryabhaṭa dates himself by it — 3600 years elapsed at his 23rd year (Āryabhaṭīya 3.10) — and dates the Bhārata war to the end of the previous quarter (1.5).

Within the hollow egg of Brahmā the planetary orbits lie one below another (Saturn outermost, the Moon lowest); in the middle the earth-globe stands in space by Brahman's supporting power, with Meru through its axis, gods above and asuras below (SS 12.29–36); the earth needs no other support and draws heavy things to itself (Siddhānta Śiromaṇi, Gola). For the Jains the luminary gods circle Meru and make the divisions of time in the human region (TS 4.12–15).

Invisible forms of time — the swift and slow apogees and the node — bind the planets with cords of air and draw them, while the wind Pravaha drives them; so arise their varied motions and latitudes (SS 2.1–8).

name: The astronomical schools (pakṣa)

definitions.definition: Siddhānta astronomy runs in schools with their own constants: the Āryapakṣa (Āryabhaṭa, Bhāskara I, Lalla, Kerala), the Brāhmapakṣa (Brahmagupta, Śrīpati, Bhāskara II), the Saurapakṣa (Sūrya Siddhānta), the Ārdharātrika (midnight) school, and later the Gaṇeśapakṣa (Grahalāghava); Varāhamihira already ranked the five early siddhāntas (PS 1.4).

notes: The pakṣa grouping is partly a scholarly (Pingree) organization of the tradition's own school names.

definitions.definition: Months are lunar (new-moon-ending in the south and west, full-moon-ending in the north) and named after the asterism of the full moon (Caitra from Citrā, Vaiśākha from Viśākhā …); a lunar month without a solar ingress is intercalary (adhika) and one with two is lost (kṣaya); solar months run from ingress to ingress (SS 1.13), and some regions (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Bengal, Odisha) keep solar calendars; the yuga, year, month and day began together at Caitra's bright first (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11).

name: The Jupiter years and the sixty-year cycle

definitions.definition: Jupiter's years are named after the month-asterism of his heliacal rising (BS 8.1–2); the sixty-year cycle, beginning with Prabhava when Jupiter rises in Māgha at the start of Dhaniṣṭhā, consists of twelve five-year yugas whose years repeat the Vedic names saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara and idvatsara (BS 8.23–29).

relations.note: the five year-names of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa's yuga reappear within each yuga of the sixty-year cycle

definitions.definition: Years are counted from the start of the Kali age, the Śaka era (78 CE, used by the siddhāntas and Varāhamihira's rules, BS 8.20–21), the Vikrama era (57 BCE), and regional eras such as the Kollam era of Kerala (825 CE); the national calendar of India (1957) adopted the Śaka era.

name: Rules for timing festivals and vows

definitions.definition: Festivals and vows are fixed by tithi, asterism or solar ingress; when a tithi spans two days the digests rule which day holds it (the tithi at sunrise, or the one covering the prescribed part of the day), and a tithi 'pierced' (viddha) by the previous one may be rejected; Vaiṣṇava and Smārta rules differ, notably for Ekādaśī (Kālamādhava; Nirṇayasindhu; Dharmasindhu; Haribhaktivilāsa).
The nibandhas (Kālamādhava, Nirṇayasindhu, Dharmasindhu) decide the right day for each rite from the extent of the tithi at sunrise and in the relevant part of the day.

notes: Rules summarized from the digests; teachings not yet extracted.

name: Sidereal and tropical reckoning

definitions.definition: Indian astronomy and horoscopy reckon longitudes sidereally (nirayana) from a fixed star-point, treating the shifting solstices as an oscillation (SS: libration of 27°); the seasons and the sun's northern and southern courses follow the equinoxes (sāyana); the difference, the ayanāṃśa, is valued differently by different schools.

notes: SS 3.9–12 on the libration from memory; not spot-checked.

definitions.definition: Bhāratavarṣa is divided into a centre and eight directional regions like the parts of a tortoise, each governed by three asterisms from Kṛttikā, so that an affliction of an asterism falls on its lands (BS 14).

The knowledge of sites came from Brahmā through the sages; a being who blocked heaven and earth was pinned face-down by the gods, who remain where they seized him, and the Creator made him the Vāstu-man, whose god-filled body lies over every building site (BS 52.1–3).

In the epic, the immortal head of Rāhu swallows sun and moon in enmity (MBh 1.17; cf. Svarbhānu in RV 5.40); the siddhāntas explain that the moon covers the sun and the earth's shadow covers the moon (Āryabhaṭīya 4.37); Varāhamihira rejects the rival accounts of Rāhu, states the shadow-cause as the truth of the śāstra, and explains that Rāhu is present at eclipses by Brahmā's boon to receive the offerings, so that the name is used figuratively (BS 5.1–15).

name: Observances at eclipses

definitions.definition: An eclipse is a time for bathing, gifts, oblations and recitation, whose offerings Rāhu receives by Brahmā's boon (BS 5.14); the digests prescribe a period of restriction before it (vedha/sūtaka) without cooking or eating, bathing at its start and end, and great merit for recitation and gifts during it; a child born during an eclipse needs a pacification rite (BPHS 91).

notes: Rules from the dharmaśāstra digests summarized from memory.

definitions.definition: A portent is a change of nature: men's misdeeds displease the gods, who produce heavenly, atmospheric and earthly portents announcing calamity; the king must counter them with pacification; the earthly yield to it, the atmospheric soften, and even the heavenly are calmed by great gifts and oblations (BS 45.1–7); moving, sweating or weeping images foretell ruin (BS 45.8). The great digest of such omens is the Adbhutasāgara.

Omens from the cries, movements and directions of birds and beasts at the start of an undertaking, classified by direction and time (BS 85–95; Vasantarāja Śākuna); the omens present at the moment of a query are part of Kerala praśna.

name: The five limbs of the almanac (pañcāṅga)

definitions.definition: The quality of any moment is read from its lunar day, weekday, asterism, yoga (27, from Viṣkambha to Vaidhṛti) and karaṇa (11), each with its deity and class (MC 1–2; BS 97–99).

name: The five classes of lunar days

definitions.definition: The fifteen lunar days repeat the classes nandā, bhadrā, jayā, riktā and pūrṇā; each tithi has a presiding deity from Agni (first) to the Moon (fifteenth); their quality changes with the fortnight (MC 1.3–4).

Every undertaking — sacraments, marriage, journeys, building, consecration, sowing — is begun at a moment whose almanac-limbs, rising sign and planetary placements suit it (MC 1–13); an act begun under ill-placed planets destroys its doer, one begun at the right time succeeds with little effort (BS 103.59–60); yet timing alone does not guarantee success (Yogayātrā 1.5).

name: The eightfold matching for marriage (aṣṭakūṭa)

definitions.definition: Bride's and groom's asterisms and signs are compared under eight heads of increasing weight — varṇa (1 point), vaśya (2), tārā (3), yoni (4), grahamaitra (5), gaṇa (6), bhakūṭa (7) and nāḍī (8), 36 in all (MC 6.21).

notes: The point values follow the rule 'each carries more than the one before' (MC 6.21); the numbers 1–8 are the standard reading.

definitions.definition: The current positions of the planets counted from the natal Moon, 'what is generally used in practice': each planet is good in certain places (the Sun in the 3rd, 6th, 10th; Jupiter in the 2nd, 5th, 7th, 9th; Saturn and Mars in the 3rd and 6th; all in the 11th) and troublesome elsewhere (BS 103.2–4); refined by obstruction-points and by aṣṭakavarga.

name: Time as a limb of the rite (Mīmāṃsā and Dharmaśāstra use of timing)

definitions.definition: Vedic rites are enjoined for fixed times — seasons, new and full moon, asterisms — so the knowledge of time serves the rite (VJ y.3); the smṛti and digests fix the times of sacraments, vows, festivals and śrāddha, and have the planets worshipped (YājñSm 1.295–308); jyotiṣa supplies the muhūrta for elective rites, while the digests decide conflicts of times.

For Mīmāṃsā, dharma is known from Vedic injunction (MS 1.1.2); the time an injunction names (e.g. spring for establishing the fires) belongs to the rite as its subsidiary; the Vedāṅgas serve the performance of the enjoined rite.

relations.note: the Vedāṅga's statement that the science of time exists for the sacrifice, extended to the smṛti rites

notes: The Mīmāṃsā definition summarizes the school's general position; specific sūtras on time as a subsidiary not extracted here.

name: Time as the condition of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa's later branches keep this purpose: the muhūrta texts fix the times of sacraments, fire-establishment, consecration and other rites (Muhūrtacintāmaṇi, prakaraṇas 5–13), and the planets are worshipped before great undertakings (YājñSm 1.295–308).

name: Number, letters and names in jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: Jyotiṣa encodes numbers in letters and words — Āryabhaṭa's alphabetic numerals, the kaṭapayādi code of the Jaimini Sūtras and Kerala, and the object-number words (bhūtasaṃkhyā) of the siddhāntas; the word horā itself is explained by dropping syllables from aho-rātra (BJ 1.3); names are drawn from the birth-asterism (VJ r.28).

name: The Tājika system

definitions.definition: Annual horoscopy (varṣaphala) from the solar return, the progressed munthā, sensitive points (sahama) and sixteen aspect-yogas with Perso-Arabic names beginning with itthaśāla; standardized by Nīlakaṇṭha (1587).

notes: The sixteen names are recalled from memory and may be misspelled or misordered.

definitions.definition: A question is answered from the chart of its moment and the omens present (Ṣaṭpañcāśikā); in Kerala the aṣṭamaṅgala-praśna uses eight auspicious objects, the querist's touch and a ritual setting, and temple queries (devaprāśna) diagnose the deity's displeasure; afflictions are traced to curses and remedied (Praśna Mārga).

name: Nāḍī leaf-reading

definitions.definition: The tradition's claim: seers wrote on palm leaves the lives of those who would one day come to consult them; the reader finds the leaf through the thumb-impression and questions, and reads chapters on the life, past births, curses and remedies.

notes: Recorded as the tradition's claim; documented practice is recent (recent: true).
